summary: For ages 12–14, teaching anaerobic respiration in animals and micro-organisms by contrast with aerobic respiration (reactants, products, energy yield, conditions). Learners write the word equations (glucose → lactic acid in animals; glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide in yeast), explain lactic-acid fatigue and oxygen debt, and see WHY incomplete glucose breakdown releases less energy. An interactive effort simulation is the lead proposed approach, with construction/explanation, a comparison poster, a coach dialogue, and a checking activity preserved as complementary approaches for different purposes.
misconceptions: Thinking anaerobic respiration releases MORE energy because it 'kicks in' during hard effort — it releases much LESS per glucose; it's a fallback, not a boost.
Believing no energy is released without oxygen — anaerobic respiration still releases some, just less.
Confusing lactic acid with the cause being 'lack of glucose' rather than lack of oxygen.
Thinking oxygen debt means you stopped breathing — it's the EXTRA oxygen needed afterwards to deal with accumulated lactic acid.
Assuming fermentation and animal anaerobic respiration give the same products — yeast makes ethanol + CO2, animal muscle makes lactic acid.

activities.title: Effort dial: push a muscle past its oxygen supply
steps: Control an effort dial wired to a single working muscle. At a gentle jog, observe aerobic respiration: oxygen in, carbon dioxide and water out, and a high energy bar.

Crank the effort up to the point where faster breathing and heart rate can no longer deliver enough oxygen; watch the muscle add anaerobic respiration on top of aerobic. The 'energy released per glucose' bar falls, a lactic-acid meter rises, and the muscle tires until you must ease off.
On stopping, keep breathing hard to repay an 'oxygen debt' gauge that stays lit until the accumulated lactic acid clears.
Switch to yeast mode and rerun the pathway as fermentation: bubbles of carbon dioxide raise dough and ethanol is produced.
Read the live comparison panel as it fills in reactants, products and energy for each mode while you drive the dial.
activities.insight: Anaerobic respiration is a lower-yield fallback that releases some energy without oxygen but far less per glucose than aerobic respiration, because glucose is only partly broken down; lactic acid build-up contributes to muscle fatigue, and the extra oxygen needed afterwards (oxygen debt) breaks that lactic acid down — which is why you keep panting after a sprint.

activities.title: Build the shared comparison and both word equations
steps: Construct a side-by-side table comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration across four columns: reactants, products, energy yield, and when it happens.
Write the animal word equation from memory: glucose → lactic acid (+ a little energy).
Write the yeast fermentation word equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
In a sentence, explain WHY anaerobic releases less energy: glucose is only partly broken down, leaving energy still locked in the lactic acid.
Write a short explanation of oxygen debt — why you keep breathing hard after stopping exercise.
activities.insight: The contrast IS the concept: no oxygen needed, lactic acid (animals) or ethanol + CO2 (yeast) instead of CO2 + water, far less energy because breakdown is incomplete, and consequences of fatigue and oxygen debt for the organism.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal comparison poster
steps: Study a side-by-side aerobic/anaerobic infographic.
Tap each pathway to reveal its reactants, products and energy yield.
Open the 'why does it burn?' flap to connect the burning feeling during hard exercise to lactic acid build-up.
After revealing, cover the poster and restate the three comparison points (reactants, products, energy) in your own words.
activities.insight: The two pathways and their products can be laid out clearly for reference and recall, giving a stable visual anchor for the contrast.

activities.title: Explain yourself to a sprint coach
steps: Take part in a dialogue where a sprint coach or sports scientist asks you to explain your own burning muscles and post-race breathing.
Answer 'why did your legs give out?' by naming the oxygen shortfall, the pathway switch, and lactic-acid build-up.
Answer 'why are you still panting?' by explaining oxygen debt as the extra oxygen needed to break down accumulated lactic acid.
Compare a steady marathon jog with a sprint: explain why the burn differs in terms of oxygen supply versus demand.

Consider a 'what if' from the coach: if you sprinted while breathing pure oxygen, would your muscles still eventually switch to anaerobic respiration? Explain that it is the RATE at which oxygen can be delivered to and used by the working muscle, not just how much oxygen is available to breathe, that sets the limit.
activities.insight: Articulating the reasoning aloud — oxygen supply → pathway switch → lower yield + lactic acid → oxygen debt — consolidates the causal chain and can surface misconceptions, including that it is oxygen delivery rate, not mere availability, that triggers the switch.

activities.title: Check the contrast and the key facts
steps: Fill in the blanks for both word equations (animal lactic acid; yeast ethanol + CO2).
Sort features into aerobic versus anaerobic columns (e.g. requires oxygen, produces lactic acid, produces CO2 + water, releases more energy, produces ethanol).
Answer a multiple-choice item on whether anaerobic releases more or less energy, choosing 'less, not more'.
Answer an item on what oxygen debt means.
activities.insight: The equations, the reactants/products/energy comparison, and the oxygen-debt and fermentation facts are confirmed and any slips surfaced.

checkQuestion: During a hard sprint your leg muscles start to burn and tire. Why can't your muscles just keep using normal aerobic respiration the whole time? Explain what changes and why the burning happens.
checkAnswer: During intense exercise oxygen can't be delivered to the muscles fast enough, so they switch to anaerobic respiration — glucose → lactic acid — which releases energy without oxygen but far less per glucose molecule, and lactic acid builds up causing the burning and fatigue; afterwards you keep breathing hard (oxygen debt) to break the lactic acid down.
